title: Pauri 31: storehouses everywhere
hook: aasan loe loe: His seat and storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all (Japji 31)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pauri 30, and your line: seen, though unseen. Did you hold someone in a friendly eye without their knowing? Today, the last of the four stanzas for the yogis. Day two hundred fifteen.

You've seen the photos: grocery shelves stripped bare because everyone got scared at the same time. Toilet paper gone, bread gone, one sad can of beans. Fear of running out makes people grab. Now hold that next to something much quieter. Cut open one apple and count the seeds. Five, maybe eight. Each one could grow a tree, and each tree could drop hundreds of apples every year for decades. One apple holds an orchard. The world is stocked in a way that's hard to take in, and most days we don't notice, because we're busy worrying about the shelves. Pauri 31 is about the storehouses.
screen: `EMPTY SHELVES.` → `ONE APPLE, EIGHT SEEDS.` → `AN ORCHARD INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Pauri 31 is short, and it opens with a yogi's word. Aasan loe loe bhanddaar. Aasan is a seat, the mat or skin a yogi carried and sat on to meditate. Wherever a yogi went, his aasan went with him, and that spot became his place. Guru Nanak says the One's aasan is loe loe, in world after world. There's no single spot to travel to. The seat is everywhere. And bhanddaar: storehouses. You've heard that word family all week. In Pauri 29, compassion was the bhanddaaran, the keeper of the stores. In Pauri 30, one of the three powers was the bhanddaaree, the one who sustains. Now the storehouses themselves are in every world. Then the line that gives us today's carry: jo kichh paaiaa su ekaa vaar. Whatever was put in, was put in once. Commentators read it as a picture of a creation already provided for: the stores were filled at the start, not in a panic every morning. Then: kar kar vekhai sirjanhaar. Having made it, the Creator watches over it, the same care we met yesterday. And Nanak signs off: sache kee saachee kaar, true is the work of the True One. The refrain closes it one last time: aades tisai aades, my salute to Him. With that, Nanak's answer to the yogis is complete. Their earrings, their meal, their horn, their seat: each one turned toward the One who is everywhere. Tomorrow, the Japji starts to climb.
screen: `AASAN — THE YOGI'S SEAT, EVERYWHERE.` · `BHANDDAAR — STOREHOUSES IN EVERY WORLD.` · `FILLED ONCE, NOT IN A PANIC.` · `THE MAKER WATCHES WHAT WAS MADE.` · then, large: `FILLED ONCE, FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Pick one place you can see or picture: a window with a tree in it, a kitchen shelf, your own hands, even the air in the room. Look at it as a storehouse. How much is in it? Leaves, light, grain, breath, years of work in your fingers. Don't count anything that's missing. Just notice what's already there, and let it be more than you expected. Then rest your eyes and breathe, one easy breath after another, drawing from a store you didn't fill. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 31. His seat and His storehouses are in every world, filled once and for all, and the Maker watches over what was made. The last answer to the yogis.
Your line: filled once, for all. Today, the next time you feel the urge to grab more, pause and look at what's already on your shelf. Day two hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Many Sikhs recite Japji Sahib each morning; Pauri 31 closes the four stanzas addressed to the Nath yogis, and its picture of storehouses in every world is often recalled as a teaching on trust and contentment.

fork.setup: a yogi carries his seat, his aasan, from place to place. where does Pauri 31 say the One's seat is?
fork.reveal: aasan loe loe: in every world. there's no single spot to travel to; the seat is everywhere.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 31: His seat and storehouses are in every world.

trapdoor: what you thought: God has warehouses.
what it means: what creation needs was placed in it, in every world, once and for all, and the Maker watches over it.
what a scholar hears: aasan is the Nath yogi's seat; bhanddaar completes a storeroom thread that runs from the bhanddaaran of Pauri 29 through the bhanddaaree of Pauri 30.

notes: Gurmukhi quoted in transliteration as the original; English is paraphrase. Macauliffe 1909 not quoted because not verified word for word.
'ekaa vaar' read as the stores being filled once at creation, following common commentary; some read it as 'all at once'. Confirm.
aasan glossed as the yogi's meditation seat (mat or skin); confirm.
Hook uses a general image of panic buying; no specific event named.
